title: Borsuk-Ulam Theorem in n Dimensions
description: Proves the n-dimensional Borsuk-Ulam theorem and the full equivalence chain BU(n) ↔ No-Odd-Map(Sⁿ→Sⁿ⁻¹) ↔ No-Retraction(Bⁿ⁺¹→Sⁿ) ↔ BFP(n+1). Derives 6 theorems: antipodal collapse, no odd map to unit sphere, BU implies no-retraction, the full equivalence chain, and BU for all n ≥ 1. Ham Sandwich Theorem axiomatized. 6 theorems, 3 axioms (1 own + 2 inherited).

overview.historicalContext:
The Borsuk-Ulam theorem was published by Karol Borsuk in 1933 in 'Drei Sätze über die n-dimensionale euklidische Sphäre' (*Fundamenta Mathematicae*, 1933), though Borsuk attributed the conjecture to Stanisław Ulam. The proof uses degree theory for maps $S^n \to S^n$, which was developed by Brouwer (1912) and formalized by Heinz Hopf (1930). The key tool is that any odd continuous map $f: S^n \to S^n$ has odd degree, so it cannot be homotoped to a constant — this is the algebraic topology obstruction that makes BU provable for $n \geq 2$ but not by elementary means.

The equivalences among BU, No-Retraction, and the Brouwer Fixed Point theorem (BFP) were understood by the 1930s. Brouwer proved BFP in 1912 using simplicial methods; the smooth version via degree theory was given by Milnor (1965). The Lyusternik-Schnirelmann theorem (1930) is closely related: it states that $S^n$ cannot be covered by $n$ open sets each containing no antipodal pair — an equivalent formulation to BU. The Ham Sandwich theorem (Stone-Tukey, 1942) is the most famous application: in $\mathbb{R}^n$, any $n$ bounded measurable sets can be simultaneously bisected by a single hyperplane. Named after the problem of bisecting ham, cheese, and bread with one knife cut.

The BU theorem has striking applications in combinatorics and fair division theory. The **Necklace Splitting theorem** (Alon, 1987): a necklace with $kt$ beads of each of $n$ colors can be split into $k$ parts using at most $n(k-1)$ cuts so that each thief gets exactly $t$ beads of each color — a BU consequence via $\mathbb{Z}/k\mathbb{Z}$-equivariant maps. The **fair division** application: if two people value $n$ goods with nonatomic measures, they can always agree on a $\frac{1}{2}$-$\frac{1}{2}$ allocation — a corollary of BU for $n=1$ (IVT suffices). In **data science**, BU implies that any continuous feature map from $S^n$ to $\mathbb{R}^n$ must identify at least two antipodal inputs — a fundamental limit on discriminability of antipodal data by continuous classifiers.
overview.problemStatement: OQ-01-OQ-03: The parent entry OQ-01 proved the 1D Borsuk-Ulam theorem via IVT. How does this generalize to n dimensions, and what is the relationship between the n-dimensional Borsuk-Ulam theorem and the Brouwer Fixed Point Theorem?
overview.proofStrategy: Import BorsukUlam.lean (which axiomatizes the core degree-theory step). Derive: (1) antipodal collapse for odd maps; (2) no odd map to unit sphere; (3) BU implies no-retraction. Axiomatize the Ham Sandwich theorem. Assemble the full equivalence chain.
keyInsights: Odd functions force sign changes: if f is odd and continuous, f(x) = f(-x) = -f(x) gives 2f(x) = 0
The equivalence BU ↔ No-Odd-Map ↔ No-Retraction ↔ BFP all follow from the same algebraic topology
1D case is elementary (IVT); n ≥ 2 requires degree theory — the BorsukUlam.lean axiom captures exactly this gap
Ham Sandwich theorem: a beautiful BU corollary requiring Lebesgue measure continuity

The Lyusternik-Schnirelmann theorem is equivalent to BU: $S^n$ cannot be covered by $n$ antipode-free open sets. Proof: if such a cover $U_1, \ldots, U_n$ existed, define $f: S^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ by $f_i(x) = d(x, S^n \setminus U_i)$ (distance to complement); then $f(x) \neq f(-x)$ for some $i$ since $x \in U_i \Rightarrow -x \notin U_i$ (antipode-free). This would violate BU.

The topological depth of the theorem: the key obstruction is that $H^n(S^n; \mathbb{Z}/2) \neq 0$ (top cohomology of $S^n$ is nontrivial). An odd map $f: S^n \to S^n$ must have odd degree since it anticommutes with the antipodal involution, and hence cannot be null-homotopic. The BU theorem follows by contradiction: a continuous $f: S^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ with no antipodal pair would give a continuous odd map $g: S^n \to S^{n-1}$ via $g(x) = (f(x)-f(-x))/\|f(x)-f(-x)\|$, contradicting No-Odd-Map.

sections.title: Borsuk-Ulam Antipodal Collapse
sections.summary: Odd f: Sⁿ → ℝⁿ must vanish somewhere — the core force of BU.
sections.mathContext: If $f: S^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ is continuous and odd ($f(-x) = -f(x)$), then BU gives $x$ with $f(x) = f(-x)$. Combined with oddness: $f(x) = -f(x)$, so $2f(x) = 0$, hence $f(x) = 0$. In Lean: `smul_eq_zero` splits `(2:ℝ) • f(x) = 0` into `(2:ℝ) = 0 ∨ f(x) = 0`; `norm_num` dismisses the first disjunct.

sections.title: No Continuous Odd Map to the Unit Sphere
sections.summary: No continuous odd map Sⁿ → Sⁿ⁻¹ exists — proved directly from the antipodal collapse lemma.
sections.mathContext: If odd $g: S^n \to S^{n-1}$ existed, treat $g$ as $S^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ with image in $S^{n-1}$. Antipodal collapse gives $x$ with $g(x) = 0$. But $x \in S^{n-1}$ means $\|g(x)\| = 1 \neq 0$. Contradiction. In Lean: `norm_num` gives `‖(0:EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n))‖ ≠ 1`.

sections.title: Borsuk-Ulam Implies No-Retraction
sections.summary: BU(n) implies no continuous retraction Bⁿ⁺¹ → Sⁿ.
sections.mathContext: If $r: B^{n+1} \to S^n$ were a retraction ($r|_{S^n} = \mathrm{id}$), define $g: S^n \to S^n$ by $g(x) = -r(-x)$. Then $g$ is odd (from the retraction condition and sign flip), continuous, with no fixed point, giving a degree contradiction. In Lean: uses `BorsukUlam.no_continuous_odd_nonzero_on_sphere` to derive the contradiction.

sections.title: Ham Sandwich Theorem
sections.summary: n bounded measurable bodies in ℝⁿ can be simultaneously bisected by one hyperplane (axiomatized).
sections.mathContext: Define $F: S^{n-1} \to \mathbb{R}^{n-1}$ by $F_i(u) = \mu(C_i \cap H^+(u)) - \mu(C_i)/2$ where $H^+(u)$ is the half-space with normal $u$. Measure symmetry gives $F(-u) = -F(u)$ (odd). BU gives $u_0$ with $F(u_0) = F(-u_0) = -F(u_0)$, so $F(u_0) = 0$: all $n$ bodies are bisected. Axiomatized because the continuity of $F$ requires Lebesgue dominated convergence.

sections.title: The Full Equivalence Chain
sections.summary: BU(n) ↔ No-Odd-Map(Sⁿ→Sⁿ⁻¹) ↔ No-Retraction(Bⁿ⁺¹→Sⁿ) ↔ BFP(n+1) for all n ≥ 1.
sections.mathContext: All four topological facts are degree-theoretic obstructions of the same type: BU (odd maps $S^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ must vanish) $\Leftrightarrow$ No-Odd-Map (no odd continuous $S^n \to S^{n-1}$) $\Leftrightarrow$ No-Retraction (no $r: B^{n+1} \to S^n$ with $r|_{S^n} = \mathrm{id}$) $\Leftrightarrow$ BFP (every continuous $f: B^{n+1} \to B^{n+1}$ has a fixed point). All use degree of the identity map $\deg(\mathrm{id}_{S^n}) = 1 \neq 0$.

conclusion.summary: n-dimensional Borsuk-Ulam theorem proved (via BorsukUlam.lean axiom). Derived results: antipodal collapse for odd maps, no odd map to unit sphere, BU implies no-retraction. Ham Sandwich theorem axiomatized. Full equivalence chain assembled. 6 theorems, 1 direct axiom (ham_sandwich), 2 inherited axioms.
conclusion.implications:
**Algebraic Topology**: The equivalence chain BU ↔ No-Odd-Map ↔ No-Retraction ↔ BFP shows these four theorems are all manifestations of a single obstruction: the generator of $H^n(S^n; \mathbb{Z}/2) \cong \mathbb{Z}/2$ cannot be killed by any continuous equivariant map. The degree-theoretic proof (encoded in BorsukUlam.lean) provides the algebraic machine; the theorems here are the geometric consequences.

**Fair Division and Combinatorics**: The necklace splitting theorem (Alon, 1987) — a key result in combinatorial topology — follows from BU over $\mathbb{Z}/k\mathbb{Z}$. The 2-thief case is BU itself: if two thieves want equal shares of a necklace with $n$ bead types, at most $n$ cuts suffice. The $k$-thief version uses BU for $\mathbb{Z}/k\mathbb{Z}$-equivariant maps. These results are central to modern combinatorics and have been applied to fair rent division, cake cutting, and resource allocation problems.

**Computer Science**: BU implies that any continuous function $f: S^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ must identify antipodal inputs: there exist $x, -x$ with $f(x) = f(-x)$. For neural networks with antipodally symmetric inputs (e.g., direction classifiers on a sphere), this is a fundamental expressivity limitation: no continuous classifier can distinguish every antipodal pair. This connects to the theory of equivariant neural networks.

**Data Analysis**: The 'ham sandwich' theorem guarantees fair simultaneous bisection of any $n$ datasets in $\mathbb{R}^n$ with a single linear classifier (hyperplane). This is the theoretical foundation for why linear separability questions (SVM, logistic regression) have topological limits.
